The drift velocity is usually divided into two components (Burger & Potgieter 1989), i.e., the combination of gradient and curvature drifts $\mathbf{v}_{gc}$ which are caused by the large scale HMF, and the current sheet drift $\mathbf{v}_{ns}$ when particles across or transport near the HCS. Gradient and curvature drifts could lead to a ~ 22-year cycle of GCR intensity and the charge-sign dependent modulation (Jokipii et al. 1977). Positively charged GCRs mainly drift inward from polar regions during $A > 0$ polarity solar cycles, and mainly drift inward along the HCS in equatorial regions during $A < 0$ polarity solar cycles. Thus drifts will produce flat and sharp temporal profiles of positively charged GCR intensity during the $A > 0$ and $A < 0$ solar minima, respectively. This effect reverses for negatively charged <!-- page 11 -->
GCRs. The detailed description and derivation of drifts for the modified Parker HMF Equation (2) can be found in Qin & Shen (2017). Magnetic turbulence in solar wind plasma causes diffusion of cosmic rays parallel and perpendicular to the background HMF. Scattering theories have been developed to describe the properties of the diffusion coefficients (see e.g., Jokipii 1966; Matthaeus et al. 2003; Qin 2007; Qin & Zhang 2014). Following Qin & Shen (2017), we use the NLGCE-F model which is in the polynomial form by fitting the numerical results from simultaneously solving nonlinear theories of parallel and perpendicular diffusion (Qin 2007; Qin & Zhang 2014). The expressions of the NLGCE-F model are as follows, $$
\ln \frac{\lambda_{\sigma}}{\lambda_{slab}} = \sum_{i=0}^{n_{\sigma 1}} a_{i}^{\sigma} \left( \ln \frac{R_{L}}{\lambda_{slab}} \right)^{i} \qquad (8)
$$ with $$
a_i^\sigma = \sum_{j=0}^{n_{\sigma 2}} b_{i,j}^\sigma \left( \ln \frac{E_{slab}}{E_{total}} \right)^j \qquad (9)
$$ $$
b_{i,j}^{\sigma} = \sum_{k=0}^{n_{\sigma 3}} c_{i,j,k}^{\sigma} \left( \ln \frac{\delta B^2}{B^2} \right)^k \qquad (10)
$$ $$
c_{i,j,k}^{\sigma} = \sum_{l=0}^{n_{\sigma 4}} d_{i,j,k,l}^{\sigma} \left( \ln \frac{\lambda_{slab}}{\lambda_{2D}} \right)^l, \qquad (11)
$$ where $\sigma$ means $\perp$ or $\parallel$, diffusion coefficients $\kappa_{\sigma} = \frac{\lambda_{\sigma v}}{3}$ and we assume $\kappa_{\perp r} = \kappa_{\perp \theta}$ in this work, $\lambda_{slab}$ is the spectral bend-over scale of the slab component of turbulence and $\lambda_{2D}$ is that of the 2D component, $E_{slab} = \langle \delta B^2_{slab} \rangle$ means the magnetic turbulence energy in the slab component and $E_{total} = \langle \delta B^2 \rangle$ is the total magnetic turbulence energy, $R_L$ means the particle's gyro-radius, and $\delta B/B$ represents the turbulence level. The polynomial order $n_{\sigma i}$ and coefficients $d_{i,j,k,l}^{\sigma}$ in Equation (8) are obtained from Qin & Zhang (2014), and the computer code for the NLGCE-F diffusion coefficients model can be found on the website at http://www.qingang.org.cn/code/NLGCE-F. According to Qin & Zhang (2014), input parameters should vary within specified ranges, shown as follows, to ensure the validity of NLGCE-F model, $$
1 \lesssim \frac{\lambda_{slab}}{\lambda_{2D}} \lesssim 10^3, \qquad (12)
$$ $$
10^{-3} \lesssim \frac{E_{slab}}{E_{total}} \lesssim 0.85, \qquad (13)
$$ <!-- page 12 -->
$$
10^{-4} \lesssim \frac{\delta B^2}{B^2} \lesssim 10^2, \qquad (14)
$$ $$
10^{-5} \lesssim \frac{R_L}{\lambda_{slab}} \lesssim 6.3. \qquad (15)
$$ Note that, to insure the values of input parameters in Equation (8) vary within valid ranges, the particle's energy should be not much more than 10 GeV and the modulation boundary of the numerical model should be set inside the termination shock (TS) (Qin & Shen 2017). Characteristics of HMF and turbulence in solar wind plasma throughout the heliosphere are needed to calculate diffusion coefficients with the NLGCE-F model. Considering two-component model of turbulence (Matthaeus et al. 1990a) in solar wind, turbulence quantities have been studied by turbulence transport models (TTMs) (Zank et al. 1996, 2012, 2017; Breech et al. 2008; Pei et al. 2010a; Oughton et al. 2011; Engelbrecht & Burger 2013). To some extent, it is complicated to apply the TTTs in long-term modulation of GCRs. In addition, the turbulence parameters in solar wind, such as $\lambda_{slab}$ and $\lambda_{2D}$, can not be observed by spacecraft directly and should be studied with some theoretical work, so their detailed knowledge is not complete (e.g., Matthaeus et al. 1990a; Adhikari et al. 2017). Therefore, we set them in simple forms according to some study for solar wind near Earth. Observational studies (Osman & Horbury 2007; Dosch et al. 2013) have indicated that $\lambda_{slab}$ is about a factor of two larger than $\lambda_{2D}$. According to new results from multi-spacecraft measurements (Weygand et al. 2009, 2011), for the slow solar wind, the correlation scale ratio of slab to 2D is around 2.6 while in the fast wind the ratio is around 0.7. Observations found that the ratio of the 2D and slab turbulence energy is about 80%:20% (Matthaeus et al. 1990b; Bieber et al. 1994), and the ratio can be different in slow and fast solar wind (Dasso et al. 2005). In solar wind and solar corona, the plasma beta ($\beta_p$) is of the order of $\beta_p \sim 1$ and $\beta_p \ll 1$, and the 2D and slab energy ratio 80%:20% is usually used in some theoretical work based on this assumption (Zank & Matthaeus 1992, 1993; Hunana & Zank 2010). In addition, the correlation scales and energies of 2D and slab turbulence may also vary with solar cycles, but it still needs some further study. Therefore, in this work, we set $\lambda_{slab}/\lambda_{2D} = 2.6$, $\lambda_{slab} = 0.02r$ (Qin & Shen 2017), $E_{slab}/E_{total} = 0.2$, and only consider the spatial and temporal changes of magnetic turbulence magnitude $\delta B$ in the heliosphere for simplicity. Note that, NLGC has also been derived into many analytical expressions, e.g., Zank et al. (2004) and Shalchi et al. (2004), which are used in many simulation models with the parallel diffusion coefficient from <!-- page 13 -->
the quasilinear theory (QLT, Jokipii 1966) as input. However, QLT is not very accurate compared to the simulation results because of the nonlinear effect (e.g., Qin et al. 2002). Based on the NLGC theory, Qin (2007) combined the nonlinear theory of parallel and perpendicular diffusion together to obtain the NLGC-E model, which is shown to agree better with simulation results than original NLGC with parallel diffusion from QLT as input. Besides, NLGCE-F also solves the case that NLGC fails in pure slab or pure 2D turbulence. For the radial dependence of $\delta B$, some studies use analytical expressions to approximate the solutions of TTMs (see, e.g., Zank et al. 1996; Burger et al. 2008; Effenberger et al. 2012; Ngobeni & Potgieter 2014; Strauss et al. 2017), and the latitudinal dependence of $\delta B$ can be inferred from the magnetic field observations of Ulysses (Perri & Balogh 2010). Based on those studies, Qin & Shen (2017) utilized an analytical expression, denoted as TRST, to describe the spatial variations of $\delta B$ as follows, $$
\delta B = \delta B_{1au} R^S \left( \frac{1 + \sin^2 \theta}{2} \right), \qquad (16)

# 1. Introduction The propagation of highly energetic charged particles in the Galaxy, known as cosmic rays (CRs) can be mathematically described by the following equation [11]: $$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} - \nabla \cdot (\mathcal{D} \nabla u) + \nabla \cdot (\vec{a}u) - \frac{\partial}{\partial p} \left( p^2 D_{pp} \frac{\partial}{\partial p} \left( \frac{u}{p^2} \right) \right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial p} \left( \dot{p}u - \frac{p}{3} (\nabla \cdot \vec{v})u \right) + \left( \frac{1}{\tau_f} + \frac{1}{\tau_r} \right) u \\
= S(\vec{r}, p, t),
\end{aligned} 
\quad (1)
$$ where $u \equiv u(\vec{r}, p, t)$ corresponds to the CR density. CRs are transported from their sources to different parts of the Galaxy primarily by means of diffusion. Anisotropic diffusion of CR particles becomes important when the magnitude of the regular (ordered) magnetic field, locally, becomes (significantly) stronger than of the turbulent fields. The significance of anisotropy of CR diffusion and the interplay physics between (anisotropic) CR diffusion and the Galactic magnetic field has been poorly understood owing to the paucity of CR observational data as well as the lack of our knowledge of the magnetic field of our Galaxy. The PICARD code [6] was developed to numerically solve the CR transport equation. Although it has been optimised to solve the steady-state transport equation, it is well-suited to handle time-dependent problems. We propose efficient solvers for the anisotropic diffusion problem which will be used in our future work to study and efficiently treat anisotropic CR diffusion in the Galaxy using PICARD. Since CR transport is a diffusion-dominated problem, we consider a simplified version of Eq. (1). The two-dimensional anisotropic diffusion equation in the presence of advection and sources reads $$
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = \nabla \cdot (\mathcal{D} \nabla u) + \nabla \cdot (\vec{a}u) + S(x, y, t), \quad (2)
$$ where $u \equiv u(x, y, t)$, $\vec{a}$ is the advection velocity, and $S(x, y, t)$ corresponds to spatially- and temporally-varying source(s). The diffusion tensor can be written as $$
\mathcal{D} = \begin{bmatrix} D_{xx}(x, y) & D_{xy}(x, y) \\ D_{yx}(x, y) & D_{yy}(x, y) \end{bmatrix},
$$ where $D_{xx}(x, y)$ and $D_{yy}(x, y)$ are the diffusion coefficients along X- and Y-directions, respectively, and $D_{xy}(x, y)$ and $D_{yx}(x, y)$ are the off-diagonal terms that give rise to the mixed derivatives in the diffusion equation. # 2. Computing the matrix exponential and exponential-like functions: Leja method We propose the use of the exponential quadrature methods [7] in combination with the method of polynomial interpolation at Leja points [1] to integrate a linear differential equation with a time-dependent forcing term, here, Eq. (2). The general form of an exponential quadrature rule reads $$
u^{n+1} = u^n + \Delta t \sum_{i=1}^{s} b_i (\mathcal{A} \Delta t) (\mathcal{A} u^n + S(t^n + c_i \Delta t)), \quad (3)
$$ where $\mathcal{A} (= \nabla \cdot (\mathcal{D} \nabla \cdot) + \nabla \cdot (\vec{a}))$ is the underlying matrix, $s$ corresponds to the number of stages, $b_i$ are the weights, and $c_i$ are the quadrature nodes. The weights $b_i$ are given as [7] $$
b_1(z) = \varphi_1(z)
$$ and $$
\begin{aligned}
b_1(z) &= \frac{c_2}{c_2 - c_1} \varphi_1(z) - \frac{1}{c_2 - c_1} \varphi_2(z), \\
b_2(z) &= \frac{-c_1}{c_2 - c_1} \varphi_1(z) + \frac{1}{c_2 - c_1} \varphi_2(z)
\end{aligned}
$$ <!-- page 3 -->
for $s = 1$ and $s = 2$, respectively. Choosing $s = 1$ and $c_1 = 0.5$, one arrives at the second-order (in time) exponential midpoint rule (Eq. (4)), given as $$
u^{n+1} = u^n + \varphi_1(\mathcal{A}\Delta t) \left( \mathcal{A}u^n + S \left( t^n + \frac{1}{2}\Delta t \right) \right) \Delta t. \quad (4)
$$ The fourth-order (in time) exponential Gauss quadrature can be obtained by choosing $s = 2$, $c_1 = \frac{1}{2}(1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})$, and $c_2 = \frac{1}{2}(1 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})$ in Eq. (3), which then reads $$
\begin{aligned} u^{n+1} = u^n &+ \varphi_1(\mathcal{A}\Delta t) \left( \mathcal{A}u^n + \left( \frac{\sqrt{3}+1}{2} \right) S(t^n + c_1\Delta t) + \left( \frac{1-\sqrt{3}}{2} \right) S(t^n + c_2\Delta t) \right) \Delta t \\ &+ \sqrt{3}\varphi_2(\mathcal{A}\Delta t) (S(t^n + c_2\Delta t) - S(t^n + c_1\Delta t)) \Delta t. \end{aligned} \quad (5)
$$ The $\varphi_l(z)$ functions are defined recursively as $\varphi_{l+1}(z) = \frac{1}{z}(\varphi_l(z) - \frac{1}{l!})$, with $\varphi_0(z) = \exp(z)$ being the matrix exponential. We evaluate the sum of the $\varphi_l(z)$ functions in Eq. (5) as the exponential of an augmented matrix [10]. This results in a significant reduction of the computational cost. We evaluate these $\varphi_l(z)$ functions by interpolating them as polynomials on Leja points. As CR propagation in the Galaxy is a diffusion-dominated problem, we consider only diffusion-dominated cases, i.e. the eigenvalues of $\mathcal{A}$ are large and negative - they lie predominantly on the real axis. We approximate the largest (in magnitude) real eigenvalue, say $\alpha$, using the Gershgorin's disk theorem, and assuming the smallest eigenvalue to be 0, scale and shift the set of eigenvalues onto the set of Leja points ($\xi$) on the arbitrary interval $[-2, 2]$. The scaling ($c$) and shifting ($\gamma$) factors are computed as $c = \alpha/2$ and $\gamma = -\alpha/4$, respectively. Now, we interpolate the function $\exp((c + \xi\gamma)\Delta t)$ or $\varphi((c + \xi\gamma)\Delta t)$ on the set of Leja points, and the $(m+1)^{\text{th}}$ term of the polynomial, so formed, is given by $$
\begin{aligned} p_{m+1} &= p_m + d_{m+1} y_{m+1}, \\ y_{m+1} &= y_m \times \left( \frac{z-c}{\gamma} - \xi_m \right), \end{aligned}
$$ where $d_m$ are the coefficients of the polynomial determined using divided differences. We use the open-source LeXInt library [3] to evaluate the matrix exponential and $\varphi_l(z)$ functions using the Leja method. ### 3. ²University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100049, China (Dated: February 13, 2024) Recent studies on cosmic rays (CRs) have reported the possibility of an excess in the antiproton flux around 10–20 GeV. However, the associated systematic uncertainties have impeded the interpretation of these findings. In this study, we conduct a global Bayesian analysis to constrain the propagation parameters and evaluate the CR antiproton spectrum, while comprehensively accounting for uncertainties associated with interstellar CR propagation, production cross sections for antiprotons and other secondaries, and the charge and energy dependent effects of solar modulation. We establish that the most recent AMS-02 $\bar{p}$ spectrum is in agreement with a pure secondary origin. Based on this, we establish upper limits on dark matter (DM) annihilation. We also determine that the AMS-02 data favors the empirical hadronic interaction models over phenomenological ones. Finally, we find that the latest AMS-02 antiproton data from 2011 to 2018 disfavors the antiproton excess at $\mathcal{O}(10)$ GeV and the corresponding DM interpretation that can simultaneously account for the Galactic Center excess in the gamma-ray observation. ## I. INTRODUCTION Antimatter investigations in cosmic rays (CRs) have critical implications for the fields of astrophysics and dark matter (DM) indirect detection. Over the past few years, significant advancements have been made in the measurement of antimatter particles in CRs. Of particular note is the Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer (AMS-02) [1], which was launched in 2011 and has yielded extremely precise CR measurements. The characteristics of CR antimatter particles have been extensively analyzed quantitatively in the literature [2], drawing on the findings of previous experiments such as PAMELA [3] and Fermi-LAT [4], in conjunction with those from AMS-02. Several recent studies have reported an overabundance of antiprotons in the flux at energies between 10 and 20 GeV, which cannot be explained by their production as secondary particles alone [5–10]. These studies proposed that the excess might be attributed to the annihilation or decay of some weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs), which are candidates of DM. The proposed WIMPs have a mass in the range of 50 ~ 100 GeV and a thermally-averaged annihilation cross section $\langle \sigma v \rangle$ near the so-called nature value of ~ $3 \times 10^{-26}$ cm$^3$s$^{-1}$, and predominantly annihilate to some hadronic final states. Additionally, several authors suggested that these WIMPs can explain the Galactic Center excess (GCE) observed in gamma-ray emissions by Fermi-LAT [11–13], and are in line with other direct or indirect DM search results [14, 15]. On the other hand, many recent studies also argued that the antiproton flux is consistent with a pure secondary origin [16–22]. At the crux of the present controversy lies the intricacy of accurately predicting the secondary antiproton flux. These antiprotons are generated via the interaction between high energy CRs and the interstellar gas, with their flux being determined by the process of CR propagation and its hadronic interaction with the interstellar gas [23]. However, both of these factors have considerable uncertainties. In this study, we present a systematic analysis of the secondary antiproton flux, wherein we deliberately consider the aforementioned sources of uncertainty. Then we can derive constraints on the cross section of DM annihilation based on the predicted $\bar{p}$ flux and the AMS-02 data. The propagation of CRs within the Galaxy is a complex process that entails diverse phenomena including diffusion, energy loss, convection, and reacceleration. Stable primary-to-secondary ratios, like B/C and B/O, are the main probes for studying CR propagation. Recent analysis utilizing high-precision data provided by the AMS-02 collaboration has indicated that a modified diffusion-reacceleration model (hereafter referred to as DR2 model) is preferred [24, 25]. However, the present measurements of CR data are insufficient to pinpoint the various propagation parameters as the uncertainties involved in secondary production cross sections can bias these parameters [26–29]. The solar modulation effect on CRs induces further uncertainties in propagation as it significantly affects low-energy CR spectra, while its precise quantification remains challenging [26, 30]. We employ the numerical tool GALPROP v56¹ [31, 32] to solve the CR propagation equation. CR propagation model Following acceleration within sources, galactic CRs undergo injection and diffusion in the interstellar medium, subsequently experiencing various propagation effects before reaching the Earth. It is commonly assumed that the propagation of CRs takes place within a cylindrical halo with a vertical extent of half height $L$, beyond which CRs are able to escape freely. This process can be described mathematically with a propagation equation [39] $$
\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial t} = Q(\mathbf{x}, p) + \nabla \cdot (D_{xx} \nabla \psi - \mathbf{V}_c \psi) + \frac{\partial}{\partial p} [p^2 D_{pp} \frac{\partial}{\partial p} \left(\frac{\psi}{p^2}\right)] - \frac{\partial}{\partial p} [\dot{p} \psi - \frac{p}{3} (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{V}_c) \psi] - \frac{\psi}{\tau_f} - \frac{\psi}{\tau_r}, \quad (1)
$$ where $Q(x, p)$ denotes the CR source term, $\psi = \psi(x, p, t)$ is the CR density per momentum interval, $\dot{p} \equiv dp/dt$ represents the momentum loss rate, and the time scales $\tau_f$ and $\tau_r$ characterize fragmentation processes and radioactive decays, respectively. Supernova remnants are widely recognized as the main sources of Galactic CRs, wherein charged particles experience acceleration through shock waves. Consequently, the spatial distribution of the CR sources follows that of supernova remnants [40]. According to the shock acceleration theory [41], the injection spectrum of primary CRs follows a power-law distribution that is dependent on the rigidity of CRs, $q \propto R^{-\nu}$. To account for the observed structures in CR spectra, a three-piece broken power law is adopted to describe the rigidity dependence of the injection spectrum [42]. The spatial diffusion coefficient $D_{xx}$ can be parametrized as [43] $$
D_{xx} = D_0 \beta^{\eta} (R/R_0)^{\delta} \quad (2)
$$ where $R \equiv pc/Ze$ is the rigidity of the CR particle, $\beta$ is the CR particle velocity in units of the speed of light $c$, and $R_0$ and $D_0$ represent the reference rigidity and normalization parameter, respectively. Although the theoretical prediction for the slope of the diffusion coefficient $\delta$ is expected to be 1/3 for a Kolmogorov spectrum of interstellar turbulence or 1/2 for a Kraichnan cascade, it is generally treated as a free parameter to fit the data. Additionally, the slope of the velocity $\eta$ reflects the possibility that the turbulence dissipation could alter the diffusion coefficient at low velocities [24]. The process of reacceleration of CRs caused by collisions with interstellar weak hydrodynamic waves can be characterized by the diffusion in momentum space, which is determined by the momentum diffusion coefficient $D_{pp}$. This coefficient is interrelated with the spatial diffusion coefficient $D_{xx}$ through [44] $$
D_{pp}D_{xx} = \frac{4p^2 v_A^2}{3\delta(4-\delta^2)(4-\delta)\omega}, \quad (3)
$$ where $v_A$ and $\omega$ denote the Alfvén velocity and the ratio of magnetohydrodynamic wave energy density to magnetic field energy density, respectively. Since $D_{pp} \propto v_A^2/\omega$, we can set $\omega = 1$ without loss of generality. Furthermore, previous research has indicated that convection is not favored by the observed CR spectrum [25]. Thus, for the purposes of this study, $\mathbf{V}_c$ is set to 0 throughout the remainder of the article. The CR spectra are greatly influenced by solar modulation below $\sim 20$ GeV. The conventional approach to address this phenomenon involves utilizing the force-field approximation, with the solar modulation potential $\phi$ employed to quantify the associated strength [45]. Introduction Observations of antiproton differential intensity spectra have long been known to be able to potentially provide valuable insights into new, fundamental physics (see, e.g., Shen & Berkey 1968; Badhwar et al. 1975; Bergström et al. 1999; Wells et al. 1999), and are an essential part of the search for dark matter (e.g., Cuoco et al. 2018; Cholis et al. 2019; Lin et al. 2019; Cuoco 2020; Osteria & GAPS Collaboration 2020). One approach to gleaning such insights is through careful modeling of the galactic transport of cosmic-ray antiprotons as is done by, e.g., Moskalenko et al. (2003) using the GALPROP code (see, e.g., Boschini et al. 2017), and for example taking into account potential signals due to dark matter annihilation (see, e.g., Barrau et al. 2005; Bringmann & Salati 2007; Evoli et al. 2015; Kachelriess et al. 2015), to make predictions as to the expected intensity of these particles at Earth. These predictions can then, in principle, be compared with various sets of spacecraft observations such as the PAMELA observations (see, e.g., Picozza et al. 2007) reported by Adriani et al. (2013b), or the AMS observations (see, e.g., Aguilar et al. 2013) reported by Aguilar et al. (2016). However, heliospheric modulation effects can greatly complicate such a direct comparison, as the various transport processes these cosmic rays experience in the heliosphere have long been known to significantly alter the antiproton spectrum (for general reviews on these processes, see, e.g., Quenby 1984; Potgieter et al. 2001; Kóta 2013; Moraal 2013). The transport of cosmic rays in the heliosphere is described by the Parker (1965) transport equation, given by $$
 rac{\partial f}{\partial t} =

$$ where $f(\mathbf{r}, p, t) = p^{-2}j_T$ is the omnidirectional cosmic-ray (CR) distribution function, as a function of position $\mathbf{r}$, momentum $p$, and time $t$, here related to the cosmic-ray differential intensity $j_T$ that is usually observationally reported (see, e.g., Moraal 2013), the solar wind velocity is denoted by $\mathbf{V}_s$, and $\mathbf{K}$ is the cosmic-ray diffusion tensor. The term $Q$ represents any sources (or sinks) of cosmic rays in the heliosphere, an example of which being the Jovian magnetosphere, an abundant source of low-energy electrons (see, e.g., Moses 1987; Ferreira et al. 2001; Vogt et al. 2018, 2020, and references therein). The terms in Equation (1) describe various physical processes that govern CR modulation: the term $1/3(
abla \cdot \mathbf{V}_s)\partial f/\partial \ln p$ describes adiabatic energy changes cosmic rays experience in the heliosphere; $\mathbf{V}_s \cdot 
abla f$ describes the outward convection of cosmic rays by the solar wind; and $
abla \cdot (\mathbf{K} \cdot 
abla f)$ describes both cosmic-ray diffusion and cosmic-ray drift due to gradients and curvatures in the 3D heliospheric magnetic field, as well as along the heliospheric current sheet (see, e.g., Jokipii & Thomas 1981; Kota & Jokipii 1983; Quenby 1984; Burger et al. 2008; Engelbrecht & Burger 2015a; Engelbrecht et al. 2019). Many studies still model heliospheric modulation effects using the force field approach of Gleeson & Axford (1968), which provides an analytical solution to Equation (1) (see, e.g., Labrador & Mewaldt 1997; Boella et al. 1998; Cholis et al. 2019; Cuoco et al. 2019; Lin et al. 2019), but this approach is not necessarily ideal, as many limiting and often unphysical assumptions (such as a 1D, spherically symmetric heliosphere in a steady state) are made in its derivation (see, e.g., Caballero-Lopez & Moraal 2004; Caballero-Lopez et al. 2019; Engelbrecht & di Felice 2020). More advanced modulation studies, which solve the Parker equation in greater detail and complexity (see, e.g., Bieber et al. 1999; Langner & Potgieter 2004; Bobik et al. 2011; Engelbrecht & Burger 2013; <!-- page 2 -->
Boschini et al. 2017) can provide additional insights into the transport of these particles, and thus into the relation between the observed antiproton intensity at Earth and the galactic spectrum. This study aims to demonstrate this, first by carefully modeling the modulation of galactic cosmic-ray protons as a function of time, using the 3D, time-dependent stochastic approach of Moloto & Engelbrecht (2020). In that study, simple observationally motivated sinusoidal scalings were employed to model the time dependences of various heliospheric parameters such as the heliospheric magnetic field (HMF) magnitude at Earth. While such an approach is suited to studying the very long-term modulation of CRs, as was the subject of that paper, the present study requires, and therefore implements, a more data-driven approach to modeling relevant heliospheric plasma quantities in order to more accurately model the temporal behavior of the CR transport coefficients, especially during the recent solar cycles 23 and 24. This is due to the fact that heliospheric parameters (such as the tilt angle and HMF magnitude) as well as cosmic-ray intensities behaved very differently during this period than during previous times in the space age (see, e.g., McDonald et al. 2010; Schwadron et al. 2010; Jian et al. 2011; Zhao & Fisk 2011; Modzelewska & Alania 2013; Zhao et al. 2014; Moloto et al. 2018; Engelbrecht & Wolmarans 2020), and that extremely accurate observations of both galactic proton and antiproton intensities exist for this period that extend to lower energies (e.g., Adriani et al. 2009, 2010, 2013a, 2013b; Martucci et al. 2018). To this end, observations of the HMF magnitude and tilt angle, as well as constructions of turbulence quantities are employed as direct inputs for the modulation model. This approach is taken as the diffusion coefficients for galactic CR protons and antiprotons are expected to be the same (e.g., Shalchi 2009), and thus a set of such parameters that yields CR proton intensities in good agreement with spacecraft observations would be equally applicable to the modeling of antiproton modulation. This model is then applied to the study of antiproton modulation, using as boundary spectra two expressions previously employed by Langner & Potgieter (2004) and Boschini et al. (2017) in the literature to study the modulation of these particles. These spectra are adjusted, based on detailed comparisons with PAMELA observations published by Adriani et al. (2013b), so as to provide estimations as to their required levels at 85 au. A section devoted to the conclusions drawn from the above analysis concludes this study. ## 2. Time-dependent Proton Modulation The present study employs a modified version of the 3D, time-dependent stochastic cosmic-ray modulation code employed by Moloto & Engelbrecht (2020). The approach followed by those authors involved the assumption of simple, observationally motivated sinusoidal temporal scalings for large scale (such as the HMF) and small scale (such as the magnetic variance) heliospheric quantities known to influence the transport of galactic cosmic rays. The present study seeks to more closely model these quantities, so as to more accurately model their influence on CR intensities. To do so, observations of these quantities from various sources (i.e., the OMNI database and the Wilcox Solar Observatory) are employed as direct inputs for the modulation code. These values are then assumed to propagate out into the model heliosphere at the (observed) solar wind speed. Stochastic Parker TPE solvers

A short time after the cosmic ray source turns off at t = 30 Myrs, the cosmic ray pressure gradient diminishes, and the momentum slightly drops. The cold gas momentum rises a bit more slowly; cosmic ray bottlenecks take time to build up (on the order of the Alfvén crossing time between the cloud and the source), and the cosmic ray pressure releases only after a long time since the cold clouds move relatively slowly. Pressure gradients on the cold gas then build to greater amplitudes and longer durations than on the hot gas, leading to a larger but more gradual acceleration of the clouds. Rather than ionization-dependent transport leading to changes in cloud acceleration, the largest changes in momentum correlate with changing magnetic field strength. ## 5. Conclusions The electron LIS derived in the current work provides a good description of the *Voyager 1*, PAMELA, and AMS-02 data over the energy range from 1 MeV to 1 TeV. The presented data for solar cycles 23 and 24 are successfully reproduced within a single framework. This includes a fully realistic and exhaustive description of the relevant CR physics. Given their high precision, recent AMS-02 electron and positron data can be used to put useful constraints on the origin of the positron excess—to be discussed in the forthcoming paper. This work complements earlier results on the proton, He, and antiproton LIS, illustrating a significant potential of the combined GALPROP-HEMOD framework. Once the covariance matrix of cross section uncertainties is known, the experimental errors of AMS-02 have to be added. The full covariance $\Sigma$ reads $$
\Sigma_{ij} = \Sigma_{ij}^{\text{cross}} + (\sigma_i^{\text{AMS}})^2 \delta_{ij}, \qquad (22)
$$ with $\sigma_i^{\text{AMS}}$ denoting the quadratic sum of statistical and systematic errors in the bin $i$.¹⁴ We can now perform a $\chi^2$ test of our predicted flux against the AMS-02 data $$
\chi^2 = \sum_{i,j=1}^{57} (\Phi_{\bar{p},i} - \Phi_{\bar{p},i}^{\text{AMS}}) (\Sigma^{-1})_{ij} (\Phi_{\bar{p},j} - \Phi_{\bar{p},j}^{\text{AMS}}), \qquad (23)
$$ where $\Phi_{\bar{p},i}^{\text{AMS}}$ denotes the measured flux in the $i$-th bin, while $\Sigma^{-1}$ stands for the inverse of the covariance matrix. For our predicted antiproton flux we find $\Delta\chi^2/\text{d.o.f.} = 1.4$ (ignoring cross section uncertainties would have led to $\Delta\chi^2/\text{d.o.f.} = 8.5$). The fit is considerably better than figure 9 suggests. The reason is that cross section uncertainties are highly correlated which could not be made visible in the figure. While the value of $\Delta\chi^2$ formally corresponds to an exclusion at $2.1\sigma$, we point out that we did not consider all relevant sources of error. Including uncertainties in the propagation and in the solar modulation of antiprotons is expected to further improve the quality of the fit. 11 Conclusion In this article we have reevaluated the antiproton production cross sections which enter the calculation of the cosmic ray antiproton flux. Compared to previous studies we have systematically analyzed proton proton scattering data of RHIC and LHC to identify the ¹⁴Here we assumed that the experimental errors are uncorrelated. <!-- page 23 -->
effects of scaling violation in the cross sections. Besides in the growth of the inelastic cross section, they manifest themselves in the transverse momentum distribution of antiprotons. The transition from an exponential to a power law dependence on the transverse antiproton mass is described by Tsallis statistics. Scaling violations are found to increase the antiproton cross sections at high energies and lead to a harder antiproton spectrum. In addition, experimental data on $\bar{\Lambda}$ production prove an increase of the strange hyperon multiplicity relative to the antiproton multiplicity towards high energies. This, in term, triggers a further hardening of the cosmic ray antiproton flux through the decay of energetic hyperons. Finally, we employed proton proton, neutron proton and proton nucleus scattering data to determine the strength of isospin effects which induce an asymmetry between antiproton and antineutron production. While the presence of isospin effects is favored by low energy data, they disappear towards high energies. We determined the energy-dependence of isospin effects and their impact on the antiproton production. Our newly determined cross sections for proton proton, proton helium, helium proton and helium helium scattering are made publicly available in the form of tables. The secondary cosmic ray antiproton flux calculated with the new cross sections was then compared to the AMS-02 data. Thereby, we kept track of all relevant sources of cross section uncertainties and determined how they propagate into uncertainties of the flux. With this article we publish the cross section uncertainties in each rigidity bin of AMS-02 as well as their full correlation matrix. These can independently be used in future likelihood analyses of the AMS-02 antiproton data. In particular, the cross section uncertainties of the secondary background are a crucial input for dark matter searches using antiprotons. Performing a likelihood test over the full energy range we found that the AMS-02 antiproton data are consistent with a pure secondary origin at the level of $\sim 2\sigma$. The fit is expect to further improve, once uncertainties in the propagation of cosmic rays as well as in the solar modulation are included. The rise of the antiproton cross sections provides the final piece in understanding the hard antiproton spectrum observed by AMS-02 at high energies.

## 6.2 Indirect Detection by $\gamma$-rays from the Halo With the problem of a lack of clear signature of positrons and antiprotons, one would expect that the situation of gamma rays and neutrinos is similar, if they only arise from secondary decays in the annihilation process. For instance, the gamma ray spectrum arising from the fragmentation of fermion and gauge boson final states is quite featureless and gives the bulk of the gamma rays at low energy where the cosmic gamma ray background is severe. However, an advantage is the directional information that photons carry in contrast to charged particles which random walk through the magnetic fields of the Galaxy [80]. For annihilation into quark-antiquark pairs, or $W$ and $Z$ bosons, the continuous energy spectrum one gets after fragmentation into SM particles can rather well and conveniently be parametrized as $$
dN_{\text{cont}}(E_{\gamma})/dE_{\gamma} = (0.42/m_{\chi})e^{-8x}/(x^{1.5} + 0.00014), \quad (131)
$$ where $m_{\chi}$ is the WIMP mass and $x = E_{\gamma}/m_{\chi}$. For more detailed spectra, one may for instance use standard particle physics codes like PYTHIA [81] (as is done in [2]). One should note that for $\tau$ leptons in the final state (131) is not a good approximation, as this gives a harder spectrum. ### Gamma-ray Lines An early idea was to look for a spectral feature, a line, in the radiative annihilation process to a charm-anticharm bound state $\chi\chi \to (\bar{c}c)_{\text{bound}} + \gamma$ [82]. However, as the experimental lower bound on the lightest neutralino became higher it was shown that form factor suppression rapidly makes this process unfeasible [83]. The surprising discovery was made that the loop-induced annihilations $\chi\chi \to \gamma\gamma$ [83, 84] and $\chi\chi \to Z\gamma$ [85] do not suffer from any form factor suppression. The rates of these processes are difficult to estimate because of uncertainties in the supersymmetric parameters, cross sections and halo density profile. However, in contrast to the other proposed detection methods they have the virtue of giving very distinct, “smoking gun” signals of monoenergetic photons with energy $E_{\gamma} = m_{\chi}$ (for $\chi\chi \to \gamma\gamma$) or $E_{\gamma} = m_{\chi}(1 - m_{Z}^{2}/4m_{\chi}^{2})$ (for $\chi\chi \to Z\gamma$) emanating from annihilations in the halo. The detection probability of a gamma ray signal, either continuous or line, will of course depend sensitively on the density profile of the dark matter halo. To illustrate this point, let us consider the characteristic angular dependence of the $\gamma$-ray line intensity from neutralino annihilation $\chi\chi \to \gamma\gamma$ in the galactic halo. Annihilation of neutralinos in an isothermal halo with core radius $a$ leads to a $\gamma$-ray flux along the line-of-sight direction $\hat{n}$ of $$

The resulting gamma ray spectrum is a line at $E_{\gamma} = m_{\chi}$ of relative linewidth $10^{-3}$ (coming from the Doppler effect caused by the motion of the WIMP) which in favourable cases will stand out against background. This is not achieved by FERMI (although data on a line search have been presented [87]). However, the Russian satellite GAMMA-400 [88] seems to have very promising characteristics for this type of dark matter search, when it is launched by the end of this decade. This could be a very interesting new instrument in the search for $\gamma$-ray lines from annihilation (or decay) of dark matter. The calculation of the $\chi\chi \to \gamma\gamma$ cross section is technically quite involved with a large number of loop diagrams contributing. A full calculation in the MSSM was performed in [89]. Since the different contributions all have to be added coherently, there may be cancellations or enhancements, depending on the supersymmetric parameters. The process $\chi\chi \to Z\gamma$ is treated analogously and has a similar rate [85]. An important contribution, especially for neutralinos that contain a fair fraction of a higgsino component, is from virtual $W^+W^-$ intermediate states. This is true both for the $\gamma\gamma$ and $Z\gamma$ final state for very massive neutralinos [85]. Note that $\lambda_{2D}$ is the correlation length for the 2D turbulence (2D integral scale, which is the characteristic length scale for the spatial decorrelation of turbulence; Zank 2014), and $\langle b_{2D}^2 \rangle$ is the corresponding fluctuating magnetic energy. The dependence of $\lambda_{\perp}$ on particle energy or gyroradius $R_L$ enters only through the parallel mfp (Equation (5)), and the inclusion of 2D turbulence is the source of the nonlinearity. Equation (7) shows explicitly the dependence of the perpendicular mfp on the energy density of both slab and 2D fluctuations, the respective correlation lengths, and the parallel mfp. Note that Equation (7) was derived under the assumption of a specific form of the 2D fluctuation spectrum, that it is constant at large turbulence scales (i.e., energy range). Matthaeus et al. (2007) have discussed different forms of the 2D power spectrum. In order to ensure a finite ultrascale (for the 2D model) as well as a finite integral scale (for the slab model), Matthaeus et al. (2007) suggest that the 2D spectrum must increase at large turbulence scales, whereas the slab spectrum needs to be flat. Shalchi & Weinhorst (2008) proposed a more general spectral form to calculate field line diffusion coefficients, which allows an increasing, a constant (which we consider here), and a decreasing spectral form in energy range. Since the behavior of the turbulence wave spectrum in the energy range is important, a more general spectrum should be employed in future studies of cosmic ray transport. ## 2.3. CR Drift Length Scale A turbulent magnetic field has been shown to reduce the effect of particle drift theoretically and numerically (Jokipii 1993; Giacalone & Jokipii 1999; Burger & Visser 2010; Engelbrecht et al. 2017). In the weak scattering limit, the drift coefficient, which enters the Parker (1965) CR transport equation through the antisymmetric part of the diffusion tensor (see Equation (1)), is given by (e.g., Forman et al. 1974) $$
\kappa_A^{ws} = \frac{\nu R_L}{3}. \qquad (8)
$$ <!-- page 6 -->
The associated divergence-free velocity for an approximately isotropic CR distribution is given by $$
\mathbf{V}_d^{ws} = \nabla \times \kappa_A^{ws} \mathbf{e}_B \qquad (9)
$$ and Equation (8). Consider the ensemble-averaged drift velocity of a particle with momentum $p$ and charge $q$ in a fluctuating magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$: $$
\langle \mathbf{V}_d \rangle = \left\langle \frac{pv}{3q} \nabla \times \frac{\mathbf{B}}{B^2} \right\rangle. \qquad (10)
$$ On using a Reynolds decomposition, the magnetic field can be written as the sum of a mean magnetic field $\mathbf{B}_0$ and a transverse fluctuation $\mathbf{b}$: $$
\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{B}_0 + \mathbf{b}. \qquad (11)
$$ Since $\mathbf{b}$ is transverse, Equation (10) yields $$
\langle \mathbf{V}_d \rangle = \frac{pv}{3q} \nabla \times \left( \frac{\mathbf{B}_0}{B_0^2} \right) \left\langle \frac{1}{1 + \langle b^2 \rangle / B_0^2} \right. \\ \left. + \frac{pv}{3q} \nabla \times \left( \frac{1}{B_0^2} \right) \left\langle \frac{\mathbf{b}}{1 + b^2 / B_0^2} \right\rangle \right\rangle. \qquad (12)
$$ If we assume $b \ll B_0$, the fluctuation vanishes when a long time average is imposed ($\langle \mathbf{b} \rangle = 0$), making the second term in Equation (12) approximately zero. Equation (12) reduces therefore to (see Engelbrecht et al. 2017) $$
\langle \mathbf{V}_d \rangle = \langle \mathbf{V}_{d,1} \rangle = \nabla \times \kappa_A^{ws} f_s \mathbf{e}_{B_0}, \qquad (13)
$$ where $\mathbf{e}_{B_0}$ is a unit vector along the mean magnetic field $\mathbf{B}_0$. Here, $f_s$ is a factor by which the value of the drift coefficient $\kappa_A^{ws}$ is suppressed and can be expressed as $$
f_s = \frac{1}{1 + \langle b^2 \rangle / B_0^2}. \qquad (14)
$$ However, most observations support a weaker assumption (i.e., $b < B_0$). In this case, the second term of Equation (12) can be written as $$
\begin{aligned} \langle \mathbf{V}_{d,2} \rangle &= \frac{pv}{3q} \nabla \times \left( \frac{1}{B_0^2} \right) \left\langle \frac{\mathbf{b}(1 - b^2/B_0^2)}{1 - (b^2/B_0^2)^2} \right\rangle \\ &\approx \frac{pv}{3q} \nabla \times \left( \frac{1}{B_0^2} \right) \langle \mathbf{b}(1 - b^2/B_0^2) \rangle \\ &\approx -\frac{pv}{3q} \nabla \times \left( \frac{1}{B_0^2} \right) \langle \mathbf{b}b^2/B_0^2 \rangle \\ &= -\frac{pv}{3q} \nabla \times \left( \frac{\mathbf{e}_n}{B_0} \right) \left( \frac{\langle b^2 \rangle}{B_0^2} \right)^{3/2} \\ &= -\nabla \times \kappa_A^{ws} \left( \frac{\langle b^2 \rangle}{B_0^2} \right)^{3/2} \mathbf{e}_n, \end{aligned} \qquad (15)
$$ with $\mathbf{e}_n$ a unit vector perpendicular to the mean magnetic field $\mathbf{B}_0$, and $\mathbf{b} \equiv \langle b^2 \rangle^{1/2} \mathbf{e}_n$. The total drift velocity, Equation (12), modified by magnetic field fluctuations, can therefore be rewritten as $$
\begin{aligned} \langle \mathbf{V}_d \rangle &= \langle \mathbf{V}_{d,1} \rangle + \langle \mathbf{V}_{d,2} \rangle \\ &= \nabla \times \kappa_A^{ws} \left( \frac{1}{1 + \langle b^2 \rangle / B_0^2} \right) \mathbf{e}_{B_0} \\ &\quad - \nabla \times \kappa_A^{ws} \left( \langle b^2 \rangle / B_0^2 \right)^{3/2} \mathbf{e}_n \\ &= \nabla \times \left( \kappa_A^{ws} f_s \mathbf{e}_{B_0} - \kappa_A^{ws} f_n \mathbf{e}_n \right), \end{aligned} \qquad (16)
$$ and $$
f_n = \left( \langle b^2 \rangle / B_0^2 \right)^{3/2} \qquad (17)
$$ is a factor by which strong turbulence introduces a new component to the drift velocity with the direction perpendicular to the mean magnetic field. From the above derivation, we can see that on the one hand strong turbulence can suppress the ability of particles to drift, whereas on the other it can lead to particle transport in a “nondrift” direction. Consequently, in the more reasonable limit $b/B_0 < 1$, there is a “drift” component normal to the mean magnetic field direction (see Equation (15)). Thus strong turbulence not only suppresses the traditional drift component but introduces a new drift component that has not been discussed. The expression (16) holds for both weak ($b/B_0 \ll 1$) and moderately strong ($b/B_0 < 1$) turbulence. It is clear that for higher turbulence levels, the standard drift coefficient would be more reduced and increased in the normal direction at high turbulence level. The derivation presented here will yield a reasonable approximation to the reduction factor $f_s$ and the new factor $f_n$. However, our emphasis in this work is not on the reduced drift effect due to turbulence, but on the recently developed 2D and slab turbulence model. Accordingly, in the following section, we will use $\lambda_A^1 = f_s R_L$ and $\lambda_A^2 = f_n R_L$ as the drift length scale due to turbulence, and we assume that $\langle b^2 \rangle = \delta B_T^2 = \langle b_{2D}^2 \rangle + \langle b_{slab}^2 \rangle$ is the total variance of the magnetic fluctuating field. ### 3. 2D and Slab Turbulence Model Zank et al. (2017) developed a set of 2D and slab turbulence transport equations for a plasma beta of order $\beta \sim 1$ using a nearly incompressible description. We use these 2D and slab turbulence transport equations to study the CR diffusion coefficients. The 2D turbulence transport equations of Zank et al. (2017) do not contain the Alfvén velocity term, in contrast to the description of Wiengarten et al. (2016).

Numerical modeling shows explicitly that in order to explain the small latitudinal gradients observed for protons by Ulysses during solar minimum modulation in 1994, an enhancement of latitudinal transport with respect to radial transport is required (e.g., Heber and Potgieter, 2006, 2008, and reference therein). The perpendicular diffusion coefficient in the polar direction is thus assumed to be given by $$
K_{\perp\theta} = 0.02K_{\parallel}f_{\perp\theta}, \quad (25)
$$ with $$
f_{\perp\theta} = A^{+} \mp A^{-} \tanh[8(\theta_{A} - 90^{\circ} \pm \theta_{F})]. \quad (26)
$$ Here $A^{\pm} = (d \pm 1)/2$, $\theta_F = 35^{\circ}$, $\theta_A = \theta$ for $\theta \le 90^{\circ}$ but $\theta_A = 180^{\circ} - \theta$ with $\theta \ge 90^{\circ}$, and $d = 3.0$. This means that $K_{\theta\theta} = K_{\perp\theta}$ is enhanced towards the poles by a factor $d$ with respect <!-- page 21 -->
to the value of $K_{||}$ in the equatorial regions of the heliosphere. This enhancement is an implicit way of reducing drift effects by changing the CR intensity gradients significantly. For motivations, applications and discussions, see Potgieter (2000), Ferreira et al. (2003a,b), Moeketsi et al. (2005), and Ngobeni and Potgieter (2008, 2011). The procedure usually followed to solve Equation (6) is described by, e.g., Ferreira et al. (2001) and Nkosi et al. (2008). ## 4.3 The drift coefficient The pitch angle averaged guiding center drift velocity for a near isotropic CR distribution is given by $\langle \mathbf{v}_d \rangle = \nabla \times (K_d \mathbf{e}_B)$, with $\mathbf{e}_B = \mathbf{B}/B$ where $B$ is the magnitude of the background HMF usually assumed to have a basic Parkerian geometry in the equatorial plane. This geometry gives very large drifts over the polar regions of the heliosphere so that it is standard practice to modify it in the polar regions, e.g., Smith and Bieber (1991) and Potgieter (1996, 2000). Under the assumption of weak scattering, the drift coefficient is straightforwardly given as $$
(K_d)_{ws} = (K_d)_0 \frac{\beta P}{3B_m}, \qquad (27)
$$ where $(K_d)_0$ is dimensionless; if $(K_d)_0 = 1.0$, it describes what Potgieter et al. (1989) called 100% drifts (i.e., full ‘weak scattering’ gradient and curvature drifts). Drift velocity components in terms of $K_{r\theta}$, $K_{\theta r}$, $K_{\phi\theta}$, $K_{\theta\phi}$ are $$
\begin{align} \langle \mathbf{v}_d \rangle_r &= -\frac{A}{r \sin \theta} \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} (\sin \theta K_{\theta r}), \notag \\ \langle \mathbf{v}_d \rangle_{\theta} &= -\frac{A}{r} \left[ \frac{1}{\sin \theta} \frac{\partial}{\partial \phi} (K_{\phi\theta}) + \frac{\partial}{\partial r} (r K_{r\theta}) \right], \notag \\ \langle \mathbf{v}_d \rangle_{\phi} &= -\frac{A}{r} \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} (K_{\theta\phi}), \tag{28} \end{align}
$$ with $A = \pm 1$; when this value is positive (negative) an $A > 0$ ($A < 0$) polarity cycle is described. The polarity cycle around 2009 is indicated by $A < 0$, as was also the case for the years around 1965 and 1987. During such a cycle, positively charged CRs are drifting into the inner heliosphere mostly through the equatorial regions, thus having a high probability of encountering the wavy HCS. Idealistic global drift patterns of galactic CRs in the heliosphere are illustrated in Figure 7 for positively charged particles in an $A > 0$ and $A < 0$ magnetic polarity cycle respectively, together with a wavy HCS as expected during solar minimum conditions. Different elements of the diffusion tensor are also shown in the left panel with respect to the HMF spiral for illustrative purposes. A formal and fundamental description of global curvature, gradient and current sheet drifts in the heliosphere is still unsettled. The spatial and rigidity dependence of $K_d$ is entirely based on the assumption of weak-scattering. A deviation from this weak scattering form is given by $$
K_d = (K_d)_{ws} \frac{\left(\frac{P}{P_{d0}}\right)^2}{1 + \left(\frac{P}{P_{d0}}\right)^2}. \qquad (29)
$$ This means that below $P_{d0}$ (in GV) particle drifts are progressively reduced with respect to the weak scattering case. This is required to explain the small latitudinal gradients at low rigidities observed by Ulysses (Heber and Potgieter, 2006, 2008; De Simone et al., 2011). This reduction is in line with what Potgieter et al. (1989), Webber et al. (1990), Ferreira and Potgieter (2004), and Ndiitwani et al. (2005) found when describing modulation in terms of drifts with a HCS tilt angle <!-- page 22 -->

Theoretical arguments and numerical simulations have been presented requiring the reduction of particle drifts, in particular with increasing solar activity. For a summary of the essence of the problem, see Tautz and Shalchi (2012). This aspect must fit into the picture where Ulysses observations of CR latitudinal gradients especially at lower energies, require particle drifts to be reduced. It thus remains a theoretical challenge to explain why reduced drifts in the heliosphere is needed to explain some of these major CR observations, and what type of particle drifts apart from gradient and curvature drifts may occur in the heliosphere. ## 4.4 Gradient, curvature, and current sheet drifts The realization that particle drifts could not be neglected in the solar modulation of CRs was elevated by the development of numerical models, which reached sophisticated levels already in the late 1980s and early 1990s including a full tensor. The importance of particle drifts in the heliosphere was at first discussed only theoretically but it was soon discovered compellingly in various existing CR observations. It should be noted that it was rather fortuitous that the sharp peak in the 1965 intensity-time profiles of CRs was followed by a really flat intensity-time profile in the 1970s, not to repeat again so evidently. The mini-modulation-cycle around 1974 had little to do with drifts (e.g., Wibberenz et al., 2001). The recent $A < 0$ polarity cycle also did not produce such a sharp peak as during previous $A < 0$ cycles as shown in Figure 6. See also the review by Potgieter (2013). Convincing theoretical arguments for the importance of particle drifts were presented by Jokipii et al. (1977) and later followed by persuasive numerical modeling (e.g., Jokipii and Kopriva, 1979; Jokipii and Thomas, 1981; Kóta and Jokipii, 1983; Potgieter and Moraal, 1985), which illustrated that gradient and curvature drifts could cause charge-sign dependent modulation and a 22-year cycle. The main reason for this to occur is that the solar magnetic field reverses polarity every ~ 11 years so that galactic CRs of opposite charge will reach Earth from different heliospheric <!-- page 23 -->
directions. This also makes the wavy HCS of the HMF a very important modulation feature with its tilt angle (Hoeksema, 1992) being a very useful modulation parameter. When protons drift inwards mainly through the equatorial regions of the heliosphere ($A < 0$ polarity cycles) they encounter the dynamic HCS and get progressively reduced by its increasing waviness as solar activity surges. This produces the sharp peaks in the galactic CR intensity-time profiles whereas during the $A > 0$ cycles the profiles are generally flatter (for recent updates see, e.g., Potgieter, 2011; Krymsky et al., 2012; Potgieter, 2013). The effect reverses for negatively charged galactic CRs causing charge-sign dependent effects as reviewed by, e.g., Heber and Potgieter (2006, 2008) and Kóta (2012). # The Impact of Particle Drifts on the Flux of High-energy Solar Protons and He Ions Arriving at Earth from Compact Solar Sources Ashraf Moradi and Joe Giacalone Lunar & Planetary Laboratory, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ 85721, USA *Received 2024 March 18; revised 2025 January 20; accepted 2025 January 22; published 2025 February 13* ## Abstract We present a numerical model to investigate the role of the ion mass-charge ratio ($m/q$) in determining the flux of MeV–GeV solar energetic particles (SEPs), released impulsively from a compact source near the Sun at 1 au. The equations of motion are numerically integrated for 0.1–1 GeV n$^{-1}$ H$^+$, $^3$He$^{2+}$, and $^4$He$^{2+}$ test ions as they move in the Parker spiral interplanetary magnetic field (IMF) carried by the solar wind. Pitch-angle scattering is included by using an ad hoc scattering operator, resulting in a parallel mean free path corresponding to “weak” scattering ($\lambda = 1$ au). Our modeled field also includes a flat heliospheric current sheet (HCS) at the ecliptic plane. We consider both A– and A+ IMF polarities and determine the time-flux profile at 1 au, at multiple observation locations, for each ion species and energy. We find that the proximity of the observer to the HCS, magnetic connectivity, and the drifts that depend on kinetic energy, $m/q$, and IMF polarity strongly impact the resulting flux–time profile. We find significant differences between the onset time, decay time, peak flux, and initial flux of the three ion species at 1 au. This contrast in the decay phase of the three species is evident in the four edges of the magnetically well-connected areas at 1 au. For magnetically poorly connected observers to the source, the onset of the proton flux with respect to that of $^3$He$^{2+}$, and $^4$He$^{2+}$ can be delayed for several hours depending on the observer’s relative heliographic latitude and the SEPs’ energy. *Unified Astronomy Thesaurus concepts: Solar energetic particles (1491)* ## 1. Introduction Solar energetic particle (SEP) events are associated with ion enhancements with maximum energies of a few hundred MeV n$^{-1}$ to a few GeV n$^{-1}$. The events with the highest intensities are nearly always associated with coronal mass ejections (CMEs). Shocks that are driven by CMEs often show increases in the flux of ions at the time of the shock passage, but only at energies much lower than the maximum energies. Thus, it is believed that the highest-energy SEPs are accelerated close to the Sun. Even though these high-energy SEP populations are low density compared to the solar wind plasma, they can pose a threat to the infrastructure both in space and the Earth, since SEPs in GV n$^{-1}$ rigidities (K.E. $\ge$ 432 MeV n$^{-1}$) are able to penetrate Earth’s atmosphere, initiate an atmospheric cascade that can reach the ground, and be detected by neutron monitors. These are known as ground-level enhancement (GLE) events. Because the SEPs at the highest energies are produced near the Sun, their subsequent motion in interplanetary space is determined by the equations of charged-particle transport, and is often simplified by assuming an impulsive release. The main transport effects that they experience are spatial diffusion, by scattering in the turbulent magnetic field, advection with the solar wind, which carries with it the frozen-in magnetic field, energy change, and large-scale drift motions. It is known that the drift motions in these high-energy SEPs are substantially larger than at lower energies, and, thus, play an important role. S. Dalla et al. (2013) analyzed the magnitude of the $\nabla B$ and curvature drifts in various heliocentric distances from the Sun in the nominal Parker spiral magnetic field under the assumption of scatter-free motion, and found that these drifts can be the source of cross-field transport for SEPs in energy ranges of a few hundred MeV n$^{-1}$ and higher. A similar conclusion was reached by M. S. Marsh et al. (2013). The effects of the $\nabla B$ and curvature drifts on the transport of solar energetic protons were also studied by N. Wijsen et al. (2020) by solving the focused transport equation in the Parker spiral interplanetary magnetic field (IMF) and the intensity profiles of 2.7–31.6 MeV protons in 0.3–1.5 au heliocentric distances for both magnetically well-connected and weakly connected observers to the injection site that was located at 0.1 au. The study focused on the decay phase of the SEP events and stated that if the observer is close to the edges of the well-connected region, the particle drifts effectively suppress the reservoir effect. S. Dalla et al. The theory provides a coherent framework in which to explore the strong or the weak scattering limits for which tractable expressions for the transport coefficients can be derived. Going beyond the scope of current WNLT and NGLC theory, a detailed cosmic-ray transport equation with expressions for the complete cosmic-ray diffusion tensor including the drift transport coefficient, as well as for convection, adiabatic energy changes, and momentum diffusion, is derived in these two scattering limits. The drift coefficient can be used to determine the modification of large-scale particle drifts by MHD turbulence. We show that if the BGK-Boltzmann approach, which is strictly speaking only valid for isotropic scattering, is modified so that particles undergo weak scattering along the magnetic field but strong scattering transverse to the field, the WNLT expressions for parallel and perpendicular diffusion (Shalchi et al. 2004) can be recovered. The expressions for WNLT appear formidable so that they are either numerically evaluated (Shalchi et al. 2004) or the more simple analytical expressions of NLGC are preferred (Shalchi & Schlickeiser 2004c; Zank et al. 2004; Shalchi 2006; Qin 2007). In this paper we attempt to demystify the WNLT expressions by taking either the diffusive or the ballistic transport limit. We find that it is possible to reduce WNLT to reproduce the simple familiar expressions for perpendicular diffusion discussed in § 2. We also illustrate analytically that these simplified expressions result in a $p^{2/3}$ dependence for the parallel and perpendicular mean free paths at lower particle energies which reproduces approximately the momentum dependence from particle simulations when 2D turbulence dominates (Shalchi et al. 2004). In addition, we discuss how the standard gradient and curvature drift coefficient for a large-scale magnetic field is modified by combined 2D and slab turbulence and how the standard momentum diffusion coefficient for slab turbulence is modified when 2D turbulence dominates. ### 4. NONLINEAR THEORY OF COSMIC-RAY TRANSPORT IN WEAK COMPOSITE 2D AND SLAB INCOMPRESSIBLE MHD WAVE TURBULENCE Our starting point is the Vlasov or collisionless Boltzmann equation for the cosmic-ray distribution function $f(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{p}, t)$ for particles with mass $m$, momentum $\mathbf{p}$ (velocity $\mathbf{v}$), at position $\mathbf{x}$, and at time $t$, which may be written in the form $$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} + \mathbf{v} \cdot \frac{\partial f}{\partial \mathbf{x}} + \mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{L}} \cdot \frac{\partial f}{\partial \mathbf{p}} = 0, \qquad (14)
$$ where $\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{L}} = q\mathbf{E} + \mathbf{p} \times \mathbf{\Omega}$ is the Lorentz force on particles with a net charge $q$. The Lorentz force arises due to an external electric field $\mathbf{E}$ and an external magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$ contained in the expression for the particle gyrofrequency given by $\mathbf{\Omega} = q\mathbf{B}/m$. In accordance with MHD theory for a highly conductive plasma, such as the solar wind, the electric field can be approximated by the motional electric field $$
\mathbf{E} \approx -\mathbf{U} \times \mathbf{B}, \qquad (15)
$$ where $\mathbf{U}$ is the plasma flow velocity. Since we are only interested in low-frequency MHD waves, this expression is of sufficient accuracy for our purpose. It is assumed that we are in the plasma flow frame where the average flow velocity $\langle \mathbf{U} \rangle = 0$, and thus, $\langle \mathbf{E} \rangle = 0$. The analysis that follows can be considerably simplified if equation (14) is transformed from the particle position $\mathbf{x}$ to the guiding center position $\mathbf{x}_g$. The guiding center position relative to the particle position is $$
\mathbf{x}_g = \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{r}_g, \qquad (16)
$$ where $\mathbf{r}_g$ is the particle gyroradius given by $$
\mathbf{r}_g = - \frac{\mathbf{p} \times \mathbf{B}}{qB^2}. \qquad (17)
$$ <!-- page 5 -->
Upon assuming that the average magnetic field $\langle \mathbf{B} \rangle$ is uniform and static with small-amplitude nonstatic fluctuations $\delta \mathbf{B}$ superposed on it ($\delta B/B \ll 1$) so that the total field $\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x}, t) = \langle \mathbf{B} \rangle + \delta \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x}, t)$ is approximately uniform and static, one finds that the guiding center velocity is (Northrop 1963) $$
\mathbf{V}_g \approx \mathbf{v} + \frac{d\mathbf{p}}{dt} \times \frac{\langle \mathbf{B} \rangle}{q \langle B \rangle^2}, \qquad (18)
$$ when neglecting the magnetic field fluctuations. By expressing the Lorentz force as $d\mathbf{p}/dt = q[\delta\mathbf{E} + \mathbf{v} \times (\langle \mathbf{B} \rangle + \delta\mathbf{B})]$ (in the plasma flow frame $\mathbf{E} = \delta\mathbf{E}$ because $\langle \mathbf{E} \rangle = 0$), the guiding center velocity in general form becomes (Hall & Sturrock 1967; Schlickeiser 2002) $$
\mathbf{V}_g = \mathbf{v} - \mathbf{v} \frac{\langle \mathbf{B} \rangle \cdot \mathbf{B}}{\langle B \rangle^2} + v_{\parallel} \frac{\mathbf{B}}{\langle B \rangle} + \frac{\mathbf{E} \times \langle \mathbf{B} \rangle}{\langle B \rangle^2}, \qquad (19)
$$ where $v_{\parallel}$ is the particle speed along the magnetic field and terms of second order pertaining to the fluctuating magnetic field were neglected. The first three terms of the guiding center velocity describe the motion of the guiding center along the actual magnetic field (uniform field with fluctuations), while the last term represents electric field drift of the guiding center across the background magnetic field due to fluctuations in the electric field. The guiding center velocity expression contains no gradient, curvature, or polarization drifts, because the fluctuations are small relative to the uniform static background field. Transformation of equation (14) from the particle position to the guiding center position yields $$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} + \mathbf{V}_g \cdot \frac{\partial f}{\partial \mathbf{x}_g} + \frac{d\mathbf{p}}{dt} \cdot \frac{\partial f}{\partial \mathbf{p}} = 0, \qquad (20)
$$ where $f$ is a function of $\mathbf{x}_g$, $\mathbf{p}$, and $t$, and $\mathbf{V}_g$ is given by equation (19) (Hall & Sturrock 1967; Schlickeiser 2002). With the aid of the second term of the transformed equation, the convection term, it becomes possible to model perpendicular diffusion and drift of the guiding center relative to the background field due to turbulence as is shown below. At first we follow the standard approach used in QLT. The particle distribution $f$, the electromagnetic fields $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{E}$, and the plasma flow velocity $\mathbf{U}$ are divided into large-scale slowly varying and random intermediate-scale faster varying parts so that in the plasma flow frame, where $\langle \mathbf{U} \rangle = 0$ and thus $\langle \mathbf{E} \rangle = 0$, $$
\begin{aligned} f &= \langle f \rangle + \delta f, & \langle \delta f \rangle &= 0, \\ \mathbf{B} &= \langle \mathbf{B} \rangle + \delta \mathbf{B}, & \langle \delta \mathbf{B} \rangle &= 0, \\ \mathbf{E} &= \delta \mathbf{E}, & \langle \delta \mathbf{E} \rangle &= 0, \\ \mathbf{U} &= \delta \mathbf{U}, & \langle \delta \mathbf{U} \rangle &= 0, \end{aligned} \qquad (21)
$$ where angle brackets denote ensemble average quantities, and $$
\mathbf{E} = \delta \mathbf{U} \times \langle \mathbf{B} \rangle \qquad (22)
$$ to first order in small fluctuating quantities, because in the limit of weak turbulence, the second-order turbulent electric field $\delta \mathbf{U} \times \delta \mathbf{B}$ is negligible. By substituting the expressions of equation (21) in equation (20) and taking the ensemble average, we get an equation for the large-scale distribution function $\langle f \rangle$ satisfying $$
\frac{\partial \langle f \rangle}{\partial t} + \mathbf{v}_{\parallel} \cdot \frac{\partial \langle f \rangle}{\partial \mathbf{x}_g} + \mathbf{p} \times \langle \Omega \rangle \cdot \frac{\partial \langle f \rangle}{\partial \mathbf{p}} = - \left\langle \left( v_{\parallel} \frac{\delta \mathbf{B}}{\langle B \rangle} - \frac{\delta \mathbf{B}_{\parallel}}{\langle B \rangle} \mathbf{v} + \frac{\delta \mathbf{E} \times \langle \mathbf{B} \rangle}{\langle B \rangle^2} \right) \cdot \frac{\partial \delta f}{\partial \mathbf{x}_g} \right\rangle - \left\langle \left( \mathbf{p} \times \delta \Omega + q \delta \mathbf{E} \right) \cdot \frac{\partial \delta f}{\partial \mathbf{p}} \right\rangle, \qquad (23)
$$ where $\langle \Omega \rangle = q \langle \mathbf{B} \rangle / m$ and $\delta \Omega = q \delta \mathbf{B} / m$.

SUMMARY AND OUTLOOK We have presented a model of the cosmic ray electron and positrons fluxes over a wide range of energies, from the MeV to the TeV domain, reproducing not only fluxes measured locally, but also the Galactic radio background and measurements outside the heliosphere. As sources of electrons and positrons we have considered SNRs, charge-symmetric extra sources and spallation processes in the interstellar medium. Moreover, we have assumed the Galactic transport of electrons and positrons to be purely diffusive. In order to motivate the spectral breaks needed in the spectrum of SNRs, we have carefully considered the influence of different data sets. A satisfactory fit to the high-energy domain of the electron and positron fluxes measured by AMS and to the diffuse radio emission can be achieved with a simple power law for the electrons injected by SNRs. However, such a model overproduces electrons at $O(\text{MeV})$ energies as measured by Voyager I. Instead, a spectral break in the SNR spectrum is required. Including in our fit also recent time-dependent electron and positron top-of-atmosphere fluxes, requires to model the effects of solar modulation, which we have performed within a simple extension of the standard force-field approximation. We have shown that the fit to solar modulated data requires the electron spectrum injected by SNRs to be steeper at $O(1-10)$ GeV energies and this makes a second spectral break at high energies necessary to fit the electron flux. In addition, the fit to the AMS time-dependent data sets has also proven that our solar modulation model works very well in reproducing the long-term trends of the low-energy electron and positron fluxes. A summary of the performance of our model in fitting the various data sets that we have considered in our analysis is shown in the left panel of Fig. 9. In the plot we compare the time-averaged sum of the time-dependent electron and positron data sets with the prediction given by the *2 breaks model*. The latter is obtained by averaging over the AMS data-taking period the flux that results from solar modulation, modelled within the extension of the force-field model presented in this paper, with parameters as in Table V. Data and theoretical prediction are in remarkable agreement.

The main purpose was to establish over what energy range drift effects could occur for electron modulation. It was found that both approaches are effective in reducing drift effects but the implicit approach is more subtle to understand. At the high energy part of the electron spectrum drift effects gradually subside with increasing energy (rigidity), which is determined by the fact that the $K_D$ and the relevant DCs scale with $\beta P$ as assumed for this work. While $K_D$ gets larger with increasing $P$ , the CR intensity gradients get smaller because of less modulation when the DCs increase, so that drift effects gradually subside as a play off between these processes. A clear value for where these drift effects become truly negligible at high energies is therefore not easy to pin down; concerning differential intensities, we find that it is between 10–15 GeV. Strauss and Potgieter (2014) reported that a recognizable difference between $A > 0$ and $A < 0$ spectra for protons appeared at 12 GeV, using their particular numerical model. In support of these values, it should be noted that drift effects are manifested in the 22-year cycles shown in observations of neutron monitor count rates at sea level at energies above tens of GeV (Potgieter and Moraal, 1985; Potgieter, 2010). This value can also change somewhat if the rigidity dependence of the diffusion process is adjusted to a steeper dependence e.g. such as $P^{1.2}$ , or when implicit reductions are applied by adjusting the two perpendicular diffusion processes, as illustrated in Figs. 5 and 6. It should be noted that all studies indicated that $K_D$ scales proportionally to $P^{1.0}$ at high rigidities, but deviate significantly from this functional dependence at lower rigidities (see Fig. 1). At the low energy side, it was found that changing the rigidity dependence of $K_D$ below $\sim 1$ GeV caused drift effects to subside rapidly because the modulation process then quickly becomes diffusion dominated. If the rigidity dependence of the DCs for electrons is also assumed as independent of rigidity, as we do here, this subsiding process is stronger. Drift effects then almost abruptly ends around 10 MeV in the inner heliosphere but at larger energies in the outer heliosphere. The maximum effect of drifts occurs around 100 MeV at the Earth (see Table 1) but at higher energies with increasing distance away from the Sun. This value can change if the rigidity dependence of the DCs is adjusted to be much different from the $\beta P$ dependence of $K_D$ . For an elaborated illustration and discussion, see Ndanganeni (2016). In conclusion, it was found that reducing drifts explicitly and implicitly does influence the energy range where drift effects are present for galactic electrons in the heliosphere. The second generation of time dependent propagation models were introduced by Potgieter and Ferreira (2001) and called the compound modelling approach. In addition to a time varying tilt angle, the temporal behaviour of the HMF magnitude, $B$, is also incorporated into this model. Charge sign dependent modulation As discussed in the previous sections, drifts will cause oppositely charged CRs to sample different regions of the heliosphere in the same HMF polarity cycle. Moreover, if we consider CR particle and anti-particle pairs, e.g. electrons ($e^−$) and positrons ($e^+$) or protons ($p$) and anti-protons ($\bar{p}$), their diffusion coefficients are believed to be the same (e.g. Shalchi and Schlickeiser, 2004) and the only difference in their transport would be their different drift directions. This makes the study of the ratios of oppositely charged CRs very useful to examine drift effects. For galactic CR propagation models (e.g. Moskalenko and Strong, 1998), reproducing the $e^−/e^+$ observed at Earth is also a validation of the parameters used in these models. Fig. 9 shows modelling results for $e^−/e^+$ and $\bar{p}/p$, taken from Langner and Potgieter (2004), for solar minimum (left panels) and solar maximum (right panels) conditions. See also Potgieter and Langner (2004). Examining the $e^−/e^+$, and similarly for $\bar{p}/p$, the ratios converge to the LIS ratio, at all radial positions, at $E > 10$ GeV as this approaches essentially no-modulation conditions (i.e. where the mean free path of these particles become comparable to the size of the heliosphere). For $e^−/e^+$, at Earth, below 0.1 GeV, the ratio again converges to similar levels for both HMF cycles. This is because drift effects diminish at these low energies and adiabatic energy losses are also generally small. The largest differences in the ratio between different drift cycles occur at intermediate energies, with the ratio generally larger in the $A < 0$ cycle. What is interesting, is that the slope of the $e^−/e^+$ at low energies at Earth is very similar to the slope of the LIS ratio (see also Potgieter et al., 2001b). If $e^−/e^+$ can thus be measured at Earth at these energies, information can be obtained regarding the different LIS levels. For $\bar{p}/p$ this ratio reaches constant levels below ~0.5 GeV, as both of these species exhibit the well known adiabatic regime, $j \propto E$, at these low energies at Earth. The level at which this becomes constant however changes during different drift cycles. Although quantitatively different, the ratios at solar minimum and maximum conditions behave qualitatively similar. See also the modelling done by Bobik et al. (2011). The process can be described by a single parameter $\phi$, the solar modulation or Fisk potential [37], which links the total energy of the particles in the local interstellar space $E_{\text{LIS}}$ to the energy $E$ observed in the detector at the Earth. The energy-differential flux $\Phi_E$ is then modulated by $$ E = E_{\text{LIS}} - |Z|e\phi \qquad (8) $$ $$ \Phi_E(E) = \frac{E^2 - m^2}{E_{\text{LIS}}^2 - m^2} \Phi_{E,\text{LIS}}(E_{\text{LIS}}), \qquad (9) $$ where $Z$ is the charge number, $e$ the elementary charge, and $m$ the mass. The modulation potential can be approximately derived from measurements of the neutron flux at Earth by various neutron monitor stations, since a strong anticorrelation is observed between the neutron flux and the solar activity [35, 38]. Nonetheless, the procedure is affected by large uncertainties. In previous works, the usual procedure was to use this value, associate with it a “reasonable” uncertainty, and use it as a prior in the fit to CR data. Here, instead, we will use a novel procedure, similar to the one implemented in [39].
